lenders.name: World Bank (IDA)
lenders.role: Road Rehabilitation and Maintenance Project (P071985), SDR 33.5 million (US$50 million equivalent) approved 9 March 2004, with a first additional financing of SDR 16.8 million (US$25 million) and a second of SDR 9.9 million (US$15 million); the completion report's cover gives the credit numbers as IDA-38660, IDA-38661 and IDPA-48210. SDR 59.98 million was disbursed. The project closed on 30 June 2014, seven years after its first closing date. The credit paid for the rehabilitation of the Chingola-Kasumbalesa road and for its engineering supervision; the completion report gives the length rehabilitated as 39 km in its results annex and as 40.5 km in its outputs annex, and the Evaluation Group's review gives the road as 40 km. The completion report rates the outcome Moderately Satisfactory and the implementing agencies' performance Moderately Unsatisfactory (27 April 2015); the Independent Evaluation Group rates the outcome, Bank performance and borrower performance all Moderately Unsatisfactory.

companies.role: Its Engineering Section moved the traders, found the new sites and valued what they lost

companies.name: Road Development Agency
companies.role: Implementing agency for the road works and the channel through which the compensation receipts were to be passed to the lender
companies.desc: Zambian state road agency, set up in 2005 under this project together with the National Road Fund Agency and the Road Transport and Safety Agency, responsible for the trunk road network.

kasumbalesa-market-traders-moved.community: In December 2005 traders were moved from the north-eastern side of the Chingola-Kasumbalesa road to the western side, to clear space for trucks waiting to be cleared by immigration at the border. The Environmental Management Unit of the Roads Department, which was responsible for applying the lender's resettlement rules, was told only after the move had happened. The abbreviated resettlement plan written afterwards, in May 2006, states that "because of lack of information and sensitization, the provisions outlined in the Resettlement Policy Framework completed during project preparation have not been followed", and that the plan was written to correct that. The plan lists 67 numbered traders by name and national registration number, some names appearing more than once, and puts the number of people at roughly 65: 23 restaurants, 20 grocery stalls, 21 sellers of vegetables, fruit and other goods, one carpentry business and two pay phones. The sums set were 2,590,000 kwacha for each restaurant, 1,390,000 for each grocery, 400,000 for each market seller, 250,000 for the carpentry and 8,000,000 for each pay phone, 113,410,000 kwacha in all. The costs counted were taking down and rebuilding structures, buying materials, business lost during the move, and transport of materials from Chililabombwe 20 km away. The plan says the host community was the same community, because the move was within the same area, and that the facilities used before the move still served the people who were resettled. The Evaluation Group's review of the completion report says the government's counterpart funding "was not paid on schedule, only six percent of the required commitments per year, causing delays in implementing the Resettlement Action Plan (RAP), and thus negatively impacting the overall project implementation timetable and costs". The same passage adds that the counterpart funding "was fully realized (US$64.3 million) at project closure as per commitment", and the review rates government performance Moderately Satisfactory.
kasumbalesa-market-traders-moved.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 67 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. The abbreviated resettlement plan's compensation table has 67 numbered entries, with three names repeating, and the plan's own text puts "the total number of people involved" at "roughly sixty-five (65)". That figure is approximate and is attached to the people being compensated; the plan's relocation sentence counts nobody, saying only that "some marketeers had been resettled". No figure in any document for this project carries a relocation verb, so none is counted here.
kasumbalesa-market-traders-moved.outcome: The plan set out that the contractor would pay each trader in front of a council officer and an officer of the Environmental Management Unit, that each would sign a receipt, and that the signed receipts would go to the Resident Engineer as part of the contractor's monthly claim and on to the Road Development Agency, the National Road Fund Agency and the World Bank. Neither the completion report nor the Evaluation Group's review of it says whether the money was paid. The completion report's table of safeguard documents records the abbreviated plan as disclosed in July 2006. The road was rehabilitated; the Evaluation Group's review says that at closing several sections, among them Chingola-Kasumbalesa, were in poor condition and in further need of repair.

kasumbalesa-market-traders-moved.confidence_note: The traders' names, trades and payment amounts come from the borrower's own resettlement plan, published by the World Bank. No independent report of the move was found. The plan was written six months after the move and sets out money still to be paid; no later document states that it was paid.

jardim-benfica-road-resettlement.drop_reason: Fails both limbs of the forward rule. The whole case was one clause of one sentence in the completion report (ICR00004791, 28 November 2019, paragraph 82): "there was effective engagement with project affected persons throughout the period, especially where the PAPs along the Jardim-Benfica Road who were displaced by the road works and were consequently relocated to a new settlement". That is no count, so limb (a) is unavailable; the batch brief records no relocation count in any outcome document for this row and none was found in one. For limb (b) the people are neither named nor counted, the new settlement is not named, and no document records anything they lost, so the entry is thinner than bukoba-airport-resettlement-arrears, where the completion report records compensation unpaid in five identified resettlement cases at a named site. Read whole, the paragraph runs the other way: the same sentence and the two that follow say implementation "was generally carried out in line with the social safeguards frameworks and plans", that the road administration's social unit "showed a strong performance in the implementation of the RAP", and that an external audit of the resettlement was rated satisfactory. The Evaluation Group's review of that report (18 February 2020, section 10a) goes further than the completion report and says that "for the rehabilitation work, no land acquisition was required and there was no loss of other assets or crops" - the completion report confines that statement to the emergency works. The only figures anywhere are forecasts: the appraisal document says impacts on housing, shops, kiosks and fences "are anticipated" along the section, and the resettlement policy framework of November 2006 budgets "resettlement for 25 structures at US$5,592.94 each" - structures, not people, and a budget line. The Jardim-Benfica resettlement action plan itself is not in the harvest, so the row can be reopened if that document is found and counts anyone.

kampala-records-centre-households-moved.drop_reason: Fails both limbs, and carried two facts that are in no document for this project. Limb (a): neither outcome document counts anyone moved. The completion report (ICR00003266, 26 February 2015, paragraph 42) says only that "since there were people currently living at the site identified for the NCRA who had to be relocated, an abbreviated Resettlement and Compensation Action Plan (RAP) was also developed", and paragraph 43 adds that the ministry "held meetings with the people residing at the site to implement the recommendations of the RAP". Neither sentence says the move happened; both state a requirement and a process. The Evaluation Group's review repeats the requirement in one clause. Limb (b): every element of harm sits in the plan, before the fact. The abbreviated plan of October 2006 says "the compensation will be paid for the 7 households before effectiveness of the project" and "physical relocation will take place as soon as the PAPs find reasonable accommodations" - both future - sets the entitlement at six months' rent, a year's crops and transport, and says "the compensation rate is in line with the established rates in Uganda". It also records that "the households do not have fixed structures or assets that could be lost as a result of relocation". That is a compensated acquisition with no count in an outcome document and no loss recorded on top of it. The one outcome statement about the safeguards runs the other way and is itself a staff statement: the completion report says that at the ICR mission "it was noted by the project environmental and social specialists that no major safeguards issues arose during the implementation of the project". Separately, two details the card carried - that two grandchildren in one household had never been to school, and that one man had no identity card, had tried once to get one and lacked witnesses - appear in no document in this project's harvest. They belong to the Morupule B resettlement plan of May 2009 (P112516, lines 123-132), another row of the same batch.

kigali-huye-musanze-urban-works-compensa.drop_reason: A count of people compensated is not a count of people moved, and nothing else on the card is a harm to identifiable people. The completion report (ICR00001375, 24 June 2010) says: "The Resettlement Action Plans have been completed and recommendations to finalize compensation taken into account. A total of 866 persons were compensated in accordance with the Resettlement Action Plans." The next sentence, which the card dropped, reads: "The June 2009 and March 2010 implementation support missions by Bank safeguards specialists confirmed that Bank safeguards policies have been respected." The Evaluation Group's 2018 field assessment repeats the 866 inside an equally favourable paragraph: "The Implementation Status and Results Reports for the project consistently rated safeguards compliance as satisfactory" and the missions "reported that the World Bank safeguards policies have been complied with". Neither document says how many of the 866 moved or what any of them lost, so limb (a) fails and limb (b) has nothing specific to rest on: land taken and compensated with no loss recorded on top of it. The 29 affected households, and the 17 on the Kabeza-Rubirizi-Isae stretch who were to move their own hedges and fences uncompensated, come from the abbreviated plan of October 2006 and are what was planned. The idle 33 hectares at Akumunigo, which the Group found serviced in 2009 and never handed out at its January 2018 visit, is an efficiency finding about project resources and not a documented harm to identifiable people; the Group gives it as a reason for lowering the outcome rating, not as a loss anyone suffered. Ratings as stated on the card were correct: the completion report and the Evaluation Group's 2011 review both rate the outcome Highly Satisfactory and the 2018 assessment lowers outcome and borrower performance to Satisfactory.

lenders.role: Shire River Basin Management Program Phase I (P117617), Credit IDA-51250 of SDR 60.6 million (US$93.75 million equivalent) and Grant IDA-H7750 of SDR 20.2 million (US$31.25 million), approved 14 June 2012, effective 7 September 2012, closed 31 January 2019; US$121.88 million was disbursed against an appraisal cost of US$142.88 million, revised to US$131.58 million. companies.role: Carried out the project through its project management unit, which ran the resettlement plan with district authorities and contractors

kamuzu-barrage-liwonde-businesses.community: The project rebuilt the Kamuzu Barrage on the Shire River at Liwonde. The completion report says the project's sub-projects did not entail physical relocation, and then records "economic displacement of 22 individual PAPs, 4 institutions (ESCOM, Maritime Police Office, Liwonde Town Council and Liwonde National Park) and 32 Fishermen at both the barrage and SRBA building". The resettlement plan of February 2014 names the people and lists what each stood to lose. One owner faced the complete closure of a camp business on the river, with a boat safari, a bar, restaurants, five guest rooms and twenty campsites. Another faced the replacement of a reception building, a bar, a house, a gate house and an old restaurant, and the loss of business income during construction. A third stood to lose the use of six shops and a dwelling house while the work went on. Eight people are listed, each losing a meat-selling business; the plan lists them as tenants of the town council's shelter and counts them elsewhere as eight households. A bicycle shed, a chip shed and a meat-roasting shed are each listed. Liwonde Town Assembly was to lose the income from six business shelters for three years, and two others the use of bare land, 0.25 and 0.35 hectares, for the three years of construction. The plan records that all of them said they were willing to give up their land provided they were properly compensated, and that they pressed to know when work would start so they could reposition themselves; the valuation team could not tell them. The project's flood-protection structures used voluntary land donation rather than purchase. A grievance system was set up and used, but the completion report says it was "gauged as partially non-inclusive to all PAPs because larger business owners did not use it", and that by project closure one grievance was still unresolved and in the courts. Elsewhere the same report says "all grievances were amicably resolved except one grievance by a lodge owner which is currently in court". The appraisal document also records that the barrage would lower dry-season water levels upstream in Liwonde National Park, reducing sandbars and floodplain grassland, and that the project area included restrictions on access to grazing in protected catchments.
kamuzu-barrage-liwonde-businesses.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 26 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people. The World Bank's completion report says the project's sub-projects did not entail physical relocation, and counts 22 individual people, four institutions and 32 fishermen economically displaced at the barrage and the Shire River Basin Agency building.
kamuzu-barrage-liwonde-businesses.killed_note: The completion report's economic annex gives 106 people killed in Malawi's 2015 floods and 60 in the 2019 floods. Those are national flood tolls, used to value the damage the project's flood works were meant to avoid; they are not deaths caused by the works.
kamuzu-barrage-liwonde-businesses.outcome: The barrage was finished and the project closed on 31 January 2019 with an outcome rating of Satisfactory. One grievance, by a lodge owner, was still in the courts at closing and no document records how it ended. In January 2026 the Malawi Freedom Network reported that lodge owners on the Lake Malawi shore in Mangochi and Salima had sued the National Water Resources Authority and the state generator EGENCO, accusing them of negligence in managing the barrage at Liwonde and saying that this caused flooding along the lake shore. That claim concerns the running of the barrage after the project closed, and it is an allegation in a case that has not been decided.

mafinga-igawa-road-deaths-displacement.title: Deaths and Unapproved Displacement on the Mafinga-Igawa Road
mafinga-igawa-road-deaths-displacement.place: Mafinga-Igawa road, Iringa and Mbeya regions, Tanzania
mafinga-igawa-road-deaths-displacement.point: OpenStreetMap node for Mafinga town in Iringa Region, at one end of the rehabilitated road section. The border post works were at the Songwe/Kasumulu crossing with Malawi, about 400 km further south.

lenders.name: World Bank (IDA)
lenders.role: Southern Africa Trade and Transport Facilitation Project, first phase (P120370), Credit IDA-52480 of SDR 138.7 million (US$210 million equivalent) to Tanzania and Grant IDA-H8440 of SDR 2.0 million (US$3 million) to the Dar es Salaam Corridor Committee, approved 21 May 2013, effective 26 November 2013, closed 31 December 2020 after two extensions; US$175.4 million disbursed. The rehabilitation of the 137.9 km Mafinga-Igawa section of the Dar es Salaam corridor took 78 per cent of the project's money; for the remaining stretch to the Zambian border at Tunduma the project paid only for feasibility studies, detailed designs and safeguard instruments. The project also financed a one-stop border post at Songwe/Kasumulu on the Malawi border, an inspection station at Vigwaza and works at eight accident black spots. The completion report rates the outcome Moderately Unsatisfactory and Bank performance Moderately Satisfactory (28 January 2022); the Evaluation Group rates Bank performance and the quality of supervision Moderately Unsatisfactory, records that the project closed with a moderately unsatisfactory rating for safeguards, and says it is not clear how the Bank "addressed the issue of fatalities related to contractors and ensured that such accidents did not repeat".

companies.name: Tanzania National Roads Agency (TANROADS)
companies.role: Implementing agency for the road works, the border post and the black spot works; began work at one black spot, including displacing people, without preparing the safeguard documents
companies.desc: An executive agency under Tanzania's works ministry that manages and maintains the national trunk and regional road network through regional offices.

mafinga-igawa-road-deaths-displacement.community: Twenty-four people died along the Mafinga-Igawa road while it was being rehabilitated. The completion report counts 104 accidents on the project road during construction, 13 of them fatal, and says that of the 24 deaths "two were attributed to the contractors' employees or involved contractors' employees and/or equipment, with the rest due to road crashes". The report puts the rate at 0.06 deaths per kilometre per year, half the Tanzanian average of 0.11 for trunk roads at the time, which it links to the slower speeds through the works, and then calls that rate "undoubtedly shocking". A road safety audit was carried out and its findings went into the road design. The borrower's comments, printed in the same report, dispute the Bank's account: they give the number as 23, say that calling it a large number "is not evidenced", point out that the report itself records the rate as below the national average, and say there is no evidence for the implied conclusion that the contractors' handling of traffic was insufficient for the traffic on the corridor. On land, the report says resettlement plans were prepared and carried out satisfactorily for most of the works, but that problems remained at closing in two places. At the one-stop border post, "compensation and demolition of property required by the implementation occurred prior to clearance of the RAP". At one of the black spot sites, "works began, including displacement without preparation of safeguards instruments by TANROADS and approval by the WB". The Bank says it kept monitoring after the project closed to ensure its resettlement policy was met and the affected people properly compensated, and that it will do so until all the resettlement issues are addressed. Other safeguard failures the report and the review record are a contractor dumping debris in wetlands and blocking water flow, and diversion roads built for the works left unattended, with erosion then affecting more than 20 km along the corridor.
mafinga-igawa-road-deaths-displacement.killed_note: The completion report counts 24 deaths along the Mafinga-Igawa road during construction, from 104 accidents of which 13 were fatal. Two are counted here because the report ties them to the contractors: they were "attributed to the contractors' employees or involved contractors' employees and/or equipment". The other 22 the report puts down to road crashes and they are not counted. The borrower's comments in the same report give the total as 23.
mafinga-igawa-road-deaths-displacement.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 17 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people. No World Bank document for this project counts the people displaced at the border post or at the black spot.
mafinga-igawa-road-deaths-displacement.outcome: The project closed on 31 December 2020 with the border post and the inspection station at Vigwaza still unfinished, to be completed with government money. The time for trucks to cross from Songwe into Malawi rose from 24 hours at appraisal to 72 hours at closing, which the report puts down to the construction still under way and to Covid-19 controls. The resettlement and compensation problems at the border post and at the black spot were unresolved when the project closed, and the project's safeguards rating at closing was Moderately Unsatisfactory.

zanzibar-drainage-deaths-compensation.title: Five Deaths and Delayed Compensation on Zanzibar's Drainage Works
zanzibar-drainage-deaths-compensation.place: Mwanakwerekwe and Stone Town, Unguja, Zanzibar, Tanzania
zanzibar-drainage-deaths-compensation.point: OpenStreetMap node for Mwanakwerekwe in Magharibi B district, Unguja. The Mwanakwerekwe pond, where two of the deaths happened, is named in the completion report; the landfill works were at Kibele in Tunguu shehia, about 13 km south-east.

lenders.name: World Bank (IDA)
lenders.role: Zanzibar Urban Services Project (P111155), Credit IDA-48610 of US$38 million approved 24 February 2011 and Credit IDA-58430 of US$55 million as additional financing in June 2016, SDR 63.9 million in all; US$87.57 million disbursed; closed 31 May 2021, five years after its first closing date. The credit paid the compensation costs under the project's resettlement plans because the government could not, and the Bank approved a further US$550,000 of project money to pay the Kibele landfill compensation. The completion report rates the outcome Satisfactory, Bank performance Satisfactory and monitoring and evaluation Substantial (23 November 2021); the Evaluation Group's review rates the outcome Satisfactory and Bank performance Moderately Satisfactory, where the completion report rates Bank performance Satisfactory. The completion report's table of supervision reports shows the project's development objective and implementation progress both rated Moderately Unsatisfactory in the report archived on 9 July 2013, back to Moderately Satisfactory by March 2014 and Satisfactory at closing; the report gives no separate rating for safeguards compliance.

companies.name: Project Management Team, Ministry of Finance and Planning, Revolutionary Government of Zanzibar
companies.role: Ran the works and the resettlement plans; took statements after each fatal accident and agreed corrective measures with the lender
companies.desc: A unit inside Zanzibar's finance ministry set up to run this project; the completion report says it had no authority over the other ministries and agencies involved.

companies.name: Zanzibar Municipal Council
companies.role: Operated the waste dump site, demolished and compensated one house to open a route for collection vehicles, and began open dumping of waste in Ng'ambo settlements after the dump site closed
companies.desc: The municipal authority for Zanzibar Town, responsible for waste collection in the urban area.

zanzibar-drainage-deaths-compensation.community: Five people died in three accidents on the drainage works between 2015 and 2020. The completion report says the project "encountered weaknesses on the implementation of health and safety issues which led to three severe accidents and five fatalities". A trespasser who broke into a drainage work site through a gap in the fence fell and drowned on 3 April 2016. Two workers died when the soil collapsed at a deep cut on 8 November 2019. Two passengers on a motorcycle died when it crashed into a dump truck working near the Mwanakwerekwe pond on 22 March 2020. After each accident the project team took statements from contractors, workers, consultants and other witnesses, reported to the lender, and agreed corrective measures; the report says site safety and health management improved after those measures. On land and money, the drainage designs were revised during the project and the number of people affected and the cost came out far above the plan; the government could not pay and no land was available for land-for-land swaps, so the credit paid instead. The report says 605 people were compensated for the drainage and solid waste works, "albeit with some delays". A further 167 people in the buffer zone of the Kibele landfill faced delays and incomplete payment because the government budget ran short; after the lender released another US$550,000, all but three had been paid by 1 April 2021. A footnote records that those three could not be reached through radio, newspapers, village leaders "and so on", and that after the loan account closed at the end of September 2021 the government is obliged to pay them if they come forward to claim. The resettlement plan of December 2018 for drainage system C counted 194 affected households and 162 structures, 30 of them to be taken completely: 141 residential structures, of which 30 would be taken entirely and 111 would lose a wall, a verandah, a foundation, a room, a toilet, an outside kitchen or a septic tank; 12 businesses to be closed and moved, among them six at Sogea and shops at Shaurimoyo, Jitimai and Magogoni; and shelters used by widows, disabled people and people with long illnesses who the plan says would need help to move. The November 2017 plan for the Kibele landfill counted 60 individual landholders, of whom 13 living in occupied dwellings, with 57 household members, were to be moved out of the project area. The municipal council demolished one house, with compensation, to open a route for collection vehicles into a dense settlement where people had been throwing their rubbish into the drain. The Evaluation Group also records that the existing dump site, which the project had assumed would last five years, was closed during the project by community opposition unconnected to the project, after which the council "began open dumping of waste in Ng'ambo settlements causing an environmental and public health crisis".
zanzibar-drainage-deaths-compensation.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 14 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people. The World Bank's completion report counts 605 people compensated for the drainage and waste works and 167 more in the Kibele landfill buffer zone. It does not count the people moved. The counts of 194 households, 162 structures and 13 dwellings come from the project's resettlement plans and are what was planned.
zanzibar-drainage-deaths-compensation.killed_note: The five deaths are counted because the completion report gives a cause for each that ties it to the works: a gap in the fence at a drainage site, a soil collapse at a deep cut, and a dump truck working near the Mwanakwerekwe pond. The report attributes the three accidents to weaknesses in carrying out health and safety measures. The Evaluation Group's review repeats all three accounts.
zanzibar-drainage-deaths-compensation.outcome: The project closed on 31 May 2021 with an outcome rating of Satisfactory. Three people in the Kibele landfill buffer zone had still not been paid when the loan account closed at the end of September 2021, and the government was notified of its obligation to pay them in future. The completion report says overall safeguards management, occupational health and site safety improved after the accidents.

lenders.name: World Bank (IBRD)
lenders.role: Morupule B Generation and Transmission Project (P112516, also filed as P116784), IBRD loan 78010 of US$136.4 million and an IBRD partial credit guarantee of US$242.7 million, approved 29 October 2009, effective 9 August 2010; US$68.88 million of the loan was disbursed and nothing was paid under the guarantee. The loan did not pay for the power station: the completion report says the government asked for it "to help finance the facilities associated with the power plant - water supply and transmission lines - and some technical assistance and capacity building activities", while the plant itself was built under an US$825 million loan from the Industrial and Commercial Bank of China, which the guarantee supported by extending its repayment period from 15 to 20 years. The report also records that the choice of technology and the selection of the engineering, procurement and construction contractor "were taken prior to the involvement of the World Bank", that the contract was signed in November 2008 and construction began on 29 April 2009, and that the Bank completed appraisal in August 2009. The power plant was nonetheless the central component of the Bank's project and the report calls it so. The loan closed on 30 June 2014 and the guarantee on 9 September 2015. The completion report rates the outcome, Bank performance and borrower performance all Unsatisfactory and the risk to the development outcome High (6 October 2016); the Evaluation Group agrees with all four ratings.

morupule-b-family-moved-fatal-accidents.community: One family lived on the footprint of the power station: a woman of 97, her daughter, the daughter's husband and their granddaughter, with a grandson who lived in Palapye and visited. Their home was two small huts built mainly of scrap and found materials, a store and a fence, on about 2,000 square metres of yard and field. They had three donkeys and a donkey cart, which they used to fetch water from outside, and they lived on firewood, mopane worms and fruit they collected and sold in Palapye and on crops they grew for themselves. The abbreviated resettlement plan of May 2009 records that they did not plant their usual food crops that year because they knew they would be moved, and that they were to be compensated for that lost harvest. Two plots were cleared for them about 5 to 6 km from Palapye, each to get a house of 3.4 by 10 metres and a pit latrine; while that was built the family was housed in tents on the plots, and the plan says they were to be moved on 25 May 2009. The family asked to stay about the same distance from Palapye so they could keep travelling there daily and keep their way of living. The plan also records that neither grandchild had ever been to school, and that the husband had no identity card, had tried once to get one and lacked the witnesses he needed. On the transmission line corridors, the completion report records that compensation was paid to informal settlers, that one house had to be demolished with its owner relocated to a nearby town, that those works, including the well fields, had an impact on about 130 households, and that two landowners complained about the compensation terms and about a borehole being moved, both complaints being resolved. The Evaluation Group repeats all of it, and adds that "the project team confirmed a resettlement action plan was prepared and successfully implemented". Five fatal accidents happened at the plant: in February 2011, August 2011, September 2012, December 2013 and March 2015. All but the December 2013 accident were falls from height; that one the report puts down to poor coordination of repairs, and the March 2015 one was a fall from height during boiler repair work. The completion report says safety remained a serious concern throughout the project, with weaknesses in enforcing safety standards and procedures, a lax safety environment, and weak control of who entered and left the site for much of the construction. An action plan was agreed after the first accident and widened after the second, after which the lender's October 2011 mission "concluded that there was a serious lack of safety observance and enforcement at the site for which the main EPC contractor should take prime responsibility". Only after the third accident did the utility suspend work at height, tighten site security and hire both a safety supervision firm and a separate scaffolding contractor; police officers were deployed to enforce site security. The environment department and the waste management department made frequent site visits and fines were levied on the utility and the contractor for breaches over hygiene, waste disposal, sewage ponds, oil and acid storage and insufficient dust suppression. Noise in parts of the plant exceeded both the contract requirements and industry standards.
morupule-b-family-moved-fatal-accidents.displaced_label: people - the family resident on the power station footprint, whose resettlement the completion report records as completed
morupule-b-family-moved-fatal-accidents.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 5 for this project. The completion report says "the resettlement of the single family of four began during project preparation and had been completed satisfactorily prior to the start of construction activities", which is where the four is counted from. The abbreviated resettlement plan of May 2009 says "one family of four is resident" on the footprint while its census table lists five family members, the fifth living in Palapye with friends and visiting. The plan and the report do not agree on when the move happened: the plan says the family was to be moved on 25 May 2009, and the report says the resettlement was completed before construction started, which the same report dates to 29 April 2009. One further household was moved from a transmission line corridor after its house was demolished.
morupule-b-family-moved-fatal-accidents.suppression: Mmegi reported on 8 January 2016 that thirty workers employed by NEPEC 11, a subcontractor at the plant, said they had been retrenched after stopping work in December over safety, pay and their contracts. They said they worked near high-voltage electricity, with dust and chemicals, and at height, without protective equipment, a risk allowance or medical checks, and that they believed they were singled out for raising their rights. The company's translator and secretariat, Jia Zhu, denied the dismissals had anything to do with the stoppage, said most of the work at the plant was finished so fewer workers were needed, and said the company had never given the workers medical examinations, not even when it hired them. The Palapye labour office had not settled the matter and set a hearing for 29 February 2016.
morupule-b-family-moved-fatal-accidents.killed_note: The World Bank's completion report records five fatal accidents at the Morupule B construction site, in February 2011, August 2011, September 2012, December 2013 and March 2015, and gives a cause for each: falls from height in all but the December 2013 accident, which it puts down to poor coordination of repairs. It counts accidents and not people, and gives no number of people killed, so nothing is counted here. Global Energy Monitor's entry on the plant, citing a Mmegi report of 30 July 2015, says at least two Chinese workers died during construction and that some Botswana workers were injured through lax observation of safety principles; that is a floor, reported at second hand, and the Mmegi report itself was not read.
morupule-b-family-moved-fatal-accidents.outcome: The plant was built but has run far below what was expected: it was meant to work at an annual capacity factor of about 80 per cent and has not. The completion report rates the project Unsatisfactory on outcome, on Bank performance and on borrower performance, and the risk to the development outcome High, and the Evaluation Group agrees. Emissions from the stacks were not measured reliably because the instruments malfunctioned or were not calibrated, and the report says sulphur oxide emissions were likely to have breached the standards whenever the limestone injection system broke down. Ambient air quality data only became available in August 2015, from a single monitoring station moved over from the older Morupule A plant.

morupule-b-family-moved-fatal-accidents.confidence_note: The two harms in the title rest on the lender reporting on its own project. The family's move and the house demolished on the transmission corridor are recorded in the World Bank's completion report and repeated in its Evaluation Group's review of that report, which adds that the project team confirmed to the evaluators that the resettlement plan was successfully implemented; no field record of either was found. The five fatal accidents are the completion report's own count, and it counts accidents rather than people. Mmegi, a Botswana newspaper, is independent of the lender but corroborates a different harm - the dismissal of thirty subcontracted workers after a stoppage over safety and pay, with the company's denial printed beside it. The only outside report of deaths is Global Energy Monitor citing a Mmegi article of 30 July 2015 that was not read.

lenders.name: World Bank (IDA)
lenders.role: Regional Communications Infrastructure Project, first phase (P094103), approved 29 March 2007. The Burundi grant closed on 31 October 2014, 27 months behind schedule; the three-country operation closed on 31 December 2016, after nine level two restructurings across the three countries. Burundi's share was Grant H283-BI, estimated at US$20.10 million at appraisal, with US$20.60 million disbursed, inside a three-country operation covering Burundi, Kenya and Madagascar whose grant estimate rose from US$164.5 million to US$249.6 million. The three countries contributed nothing of the US$37.40 million expected of them. The Evaluation Group rates the outcome Moderately Satisfactory and Bank performance Moderately Satisfactory.

companies.name: Burundi Backbone System (BBS)
companies.role: The company that built and ran the national fibre network under the project; the state revoked its public-private status and nationalised it in January 2017
companies.desc: A Burundian company set up under this project with private sector participation to build and operate the national fibre backbone and sell capacity to operators.

burundi-fibre-backbone-unpaid-compensati.community: The project laid 1,254 km of fibre optic cable across Burundi, reaching 34 communes, and linked 58 government institutions and 14 universities. The Evaluation Group's review of the completion report says that in Burundi "compensations were paid in full for 8,265 people for a total amount of Burundian Franc (BIF) 105,311,800 (equivalent of approximately US$67,000 in April 2015)", and that "115 people were yet to be paid compensation at project closure". The documents do not say what the 8,265 people lost, do not break the sum down, and do not say why the 115 were not paid. In Kenya the review says no resettlement was needed. In Madagascar compensation was paid in full, US$56,941 under the resettlement plan and US$9,241 under the environmental and social management plan; the resettlement plan of July 2012 for zones 1A and 2 covers four affected people at four of the 68 sites, with a budget of 43,562,500 ariary, and records that at one site only two households were involved so the survey results did not have to be posted publicly.
burundi-fibre-backbone-unpaid-compensati.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 1 for this project. The Evaluation Group's review counts 8,265 people compensated in Burundi and 115 still unpaid at closing; no document counts anyone moved.
burundi-fibre-backbone-unpaid-compensati.outcome: The network was working when the project closed. The review records that the authorities revoked the public-private status of Burundi Backbone System and nationalised it in January 2017, "without consultation or compensation", officially on the grounds that the shareholders were not respecting their contractual terms, and rates the sustainability risk Significant for that reason. No document says whether the 115 people were ever paid.

burundi-fibre-backbone-unpaid-compensati.confidence_note: The figures rest on the Evaluation Group's review of a completion report that the Bank's document archive does not return under this project number; the review cites that report by page. The review gives the Burundi total as 8,265 people compensated for 105,311,800 Burundian francs and does not break the sum down per person, say what was lost, or say what became of the 115 unpaid. No independent report was found.

mutundwe-thermal-plant-land-and-homes.drop_reason: The only named person is a forecast and the only outcome sentence is a list of mitigation measures. The resettlement plan of November 2006 is wholly prospective: "The construction of the thermal-power plant to curb the power shortage experienced in various parts of the country will affect one lady in a negative manner. This will be in form of loss of land and crops." The same plan says no homestead would be displaced. One acre of mailo land and its crops, to be compensated, is a compensated acquisition with no loss recorded on top of it and no count in an outcome document. The completion report (ICR2159, 31 March 2012) does not record a relocation as an outcome. Its paragraph 36 opens "The project complied with the identified safeguard policies (OP 4.01 and 4.12) at both preparation and implementation phases" and the only relevant sentence is a list: "Other mitigation measures included compensation and resettlement for residents near the plant in other areas for the duration of the PPA; construction of a 5m noise barrier to reduce noise levels; changing the lighting system, re-scheduling the ignition times to minimize the ADO smell at ignition and monitoring of households that were resettled out of the plant site." The relocation word sits inside the description of a monitoring measure, with no count, no place, no amount and no loss, and the paragraph it sits in is a compliance finding. That is thinner than bukoba-airport-resettlement-arrears, where the completion report records compensation unpaid in five identified resettlement cases at a named site. The Evaluation Group's review adds only that the report "does not contain information on the degree of satisfaction of project-affected persons with their compensation and resettlement arrangements", which is an absence and not a harm. Worth keeping with the row for any later reopening: the plan and the report flatly disagree about whether any homestead was displaced, and nobody reconciles them.

imusho-village-moved-from-national-park.drop_reason: A compensated, agreed relocation with no count in an outcome document and no loss recorded on top of the move. The completion report (ICR00002238, 29 June 2012, paragraph 50) is the only outcome document on it and says in full: "A Resettlement Action Plan (RAP) was prepared to guide resettlement of the inhabitants of a village called Imusho located within the MNP. Guided by the RAP, resettlement took place prior effectiveness. It included adequate compensation as determined by a Bank social specialist." No count, so limb (a) fails; the figures of 35 adult men, 12 adult women and 13 children are the September 2003 plan's census of the village in November 2001, before the move. For limb (b) the plan records the move as agreed after meetings with the village, with title to 233.53 hectares at the new site, compensation for buildings and fruit trees at replacement cost without depreciation and paid before anyone moved, transport provided, and leave for anyone who chose to stay to do so by agreement. No document records anything lost on top of that. The elephant that killed a woman within the village site in June 2003 is given by the plan as a reason for moving and was not caused by the works. The project's other displacement, in the Namwala Game Management Area, is uncounted, is attributed by the completion report to "an instruction issued by the land chiefs" rather than to project works, and the same paragraph records the Bank's conclusion that there was no non-compliance because its resettlement policy "does not apply to restrictions of access to natural resources under community-based projects". Worth recording for any reopening: the move predates the credit's effectiveness of 10 November 2004, the plan was prepared for this project and cleared by the lender, and the completion report's own output table lists "Resettlement of Imusho village prior effectiveness" as a project output, so the timing test is met even though the forward rule is not. The third volume of the project's resettlement papers, an aide memoire that might record what happened to the village after the move, is still unread - see the check log for the route that failed.

p075997-cape-biodiversity-coleske.drop_reason: No one was moved and the loss of work that the people suffered came from a land purchase the project did not finance. The ICIJ figure of 35 is the 35 households of former farm workers at Coleske, inside the core zone of the Baviaanskloof Mega-Reserve, whose resettlement the project planned for and never carried out. The Evaluation Group's review says the proposed resettlement of the Coleske farm workers "was not completed by project close". The completion report (25 April 2011, para 37-39) says "a segment of the Coleske community has continued to decline ECBP's resettlement offers", that without their agreement the Eastern Cape Parks Board "has not yet moved forward with the option of seeking a court order that would require the resettlement to take place", and that the project "did not include funding for any such resettlement", which would be paid for with government money if it ever happened. The same paragraphs record that Coleske Farm was bought by the Eastern Cape department in 2001, "well before the start of the BCSD project", between willing buyer and willing seller, that no provision was made for the farm's agricultural workers and that none of them hold land ownership rights under South African law. On the outcome for those people the report says the final Bank mission visited the site, met many of the residents and concluded that the project had adequately addressed their livelihood concerns, that the parks board agreed specific uses of natural resources inside the reserve and gave Coleske residents preference for work including 10 staff jobs, and that the residents "have thus been able to maintain or improve their livelihoods" while waiting for the government's decision. The Evaluation Group's review repeats all of this. Checked against the outcome documents: the completion report's own safeguards section says that for the rest of the project the resettlement and process frameworks were not needed because protected area expansion came from re-assigned state forestry land and voluntary stewardship agreements, and that marine zoning followed the process framework, giving Betty's Bay as an example agreed with local stakeholders. Two outside documents by the same author point the other way and are recorded here so the row can be reopened: a April 2009 paper by Eleanor Macgregor of the Wilderness Foundation, published on the implementing agency's website, says eight people had held permanent jobs on the farm with more than 100 dependents between them, that temporary work was arranged for 40 people when the farm was bought, that residents had used the land for grazing donkeys, acacia wood, medicinal plants and honey, that the department was legally bound only to offer equivalent housing in the nearest town about 100 km away, and that Willowmore and Steytlerville have extremely high unemployment; and the same author's 2014 master's dissertation at the University of the Free State finds that "the general situation of Coleske has deteriorated" since the land was bought. Both describe harm that begins with the 2001 purchase, which this GEF grant did not finance, and neither records anyone being moved.

p126579-eastern-electricity-highway.note: Confirmed by place and years as well as by P-number: the existing case covers the Kenya side of the Eastern Electricity Highway from Laikipia to Suswa, 2017 to 2024, and already carries the 2,638 affected people, the 832 still owed land compensation at closing in January 2024, the 96 and 13 still owed for crops and structures in April 2024, the two fatal accidents, the 200 families who lost communal grazing land and the livestock feed plant. The documents harvested for this round add no fact that is not already in the existing case. The 2016 resettlement plan on disk gives plan figures only: 345 people in 52 households losing farmland and trees at the ground electrode site, and around 200 households, about 1,000 people, counted as using the communal grazing area.
